entities.body: The other half of Torry and Alexander, the revival that worked Dublin last year. Bloom remembers the pair as one act and does not separate them; the name is his measure of how often this trade comes round.

entities.name: Dedalus’s daughter
entities.body: Lobbing about outside Dillon’s auctionrooms on Bachelor’s walk, waiting for her father, with some old furniture going under the hammer inside. Bloom knows her eyes at once from the father, counts the fifteen children, and notes the dress in flitters and the underfed look of her. The episode does not give her a first name.

entities.name: The old applewoman
entities.body: Two apples a penny, two for a penny, at the corner of the bridge. Bloom buys two Banbury cakes from her for a penny and breaks them up for the gulls, who take every morsel and give him not even a caw.

entities.name: Dr Hy Franks
entities.body: The quack for the clap whose strictly confidential bills used to be stuck up in all the greenhouses, and who never paid a red for the privilege. Bloom the canvasser reads the city as a hoarding and grades the work.

entities.name: Maginni
entities.body: The dancing master, whose self advertisement Bloom sets against Franks: he got fellows to stick the bills up, or stuck them up himself on the q. t., running in to loosen a button.

entities.name: Sir Robert Ball
entities.body: Whose fascinating little book gave Bloom the word parallax, which he has never exactly understood, and which comes back at him all day. Par it’s Greek: parallel, parallax.

entities.name: The Y of Hely’s
entities.body: Fifth of the whitesmocked sandwichmen with the scarlet sashes, lagging behind the others along the gutter and eating a chunk of bread from under his foreboard as he walks. Three bob a day, Bloom reckons, street after street: just keep skin and bone together.

entities.name: M’Glade
entities.body: Whose men the sandwichboard procession turns out to be. Doesn’t bring in any business either, Bloom decides, and goes back over the showcart with two smart girls in it that Hely would not have because he had not thought of it himself.

entities.name: The nun at Tranquilla
entities.body: A really sweet face, the wimple suiting her small head, whom Bloom disturbed at her devotions the morning he came to collect the convent’s account. Our great day, she said: feast of Our Lady of Mount Carmel. She knew, he thinks — I think she knew by the way she.

entities.name: Pat Claffey
entities.body: The pawnbroker’s daughter, the name Bloom gropes for when he cannot think what the nun was called. Sister? Sister? Pat Claffey. It is offered as a guess and the episode never settles it.

entities.name: Phil Gilligan
entities.body: By whose death Bloom dates the year: ninetyfour, the big fire at Arnott’s, when they were in Lombard street west and Milly was a kiddy.

entities.name: Val Dillon
entities.body: Lord mayor at the Glencree dinner, the night Molly wore the elephantgrey dress with the braided frogs and people looked after her.

entities.name: Alderman Robert O’Reilly
entities.body: Who emptied the port into his soup before the flag fell at that same dinner, and lapped it up for the inner alderman. Bobbob.

entities.name: Bartell d’Arcy
entities.body: The tenor, just coming out then, conceited with his waxedup moustache, who saw Molly home after practice and gave her Winds that blow from the south. Bloom leaves the thought there and moves to the windy night he went to fetch her himself.

entities.name: Mrs Breen
entities.body: Josie Powell that was, of the charades at Luke Doyle’s in Dolphin’s Barn, only a year or so older than Molly and wearing the same blue serge dress as two years ago, the nap bleaching. She stops Bloom on Westmoreland street, hears about Dignam, and shows him the postcard her husband got.

entities.name: Denis Breen
entities.body: Her lord and master, a caution to rattlesnakes, in there now with his lawbooks finding out the law of libel. He woke her in the night to say the ace of spades was walking up the stairs, and he shuffles out of Harrison’s in a skimpy frockcoat and blue canvas shoes with two heavy tomes under his arm, bound for Menton’s office and an action for ten thousand pounds.

entities.name: Lot’s wife
entities.body: Who looked back and was turned to a pillar of salt, in the two words Joyce gives the thought about women’s curiosity: Pillar of salt. Only the modern edition supplies the name, which is why she is unreachable in the older text.

entities.name: The barefoot arab
entities.body: Standing over the grating outside Harrison’s breathing in the noonreek of mockturtle and jampuffs. Deaden the gnaw of hunger that way, Bloom thinks. Pleasure or pain is it?

entities.name: Luke Doyle
entities.body: In whose house at Dolphin’s Barn the charades were played, long ago, where Bloom first knew Josie Powell. U. p: up comes back to him out of the same evening.

entities.name: Mina Purefoy
entities.body: Three days bad in the lying-in hospital in Holles street, with a houseful of kids at home and a very stiff birth, the nurse told Mrs Breen. Bloom asks after her under the wrong name, Mrs Beaufoy, because Philip Beaufoy of the prize titbit is in his head; and she stays in his head for the rest of the episode.

entities.name: Theodore Purefoy
entities.body: The Methodist husband. Method in his madness: saffron bun and milk and soda in the educational dairy, eating with a stopwatch, thirtytwo chews to the minute, and hardy annuals he presents her with. Bloom saw him marching bareheaded out at the Three Jolly Topers with his eldest boy carrying one in a marketnet.

entities.name: Dr Horne
entities.body: Master of the lying-in hospital in Holles street, who got Mrs Purefoy in. Bloom hears the name from Mrs Breen and keeps it with the three days and the forceps.

entities.name: Cashel Boyle O’Connor Fitzmaurice Tisdall Farrell
entities.body: The bony form who strides along the curbstone staring through a heavystringed glass, a tiny hat gripped tight as a skullpiece on his head, a dustcoat and stick and umbrella dangling from his arm. He always walks outside the lampposts. He has enough of them, Mrs Breen says of the names.
aliases: Cashel Boyle O’Connor Fitzmaurice Tisdall Farrell
Cashel Boyle O'Connor Fitzmaurice Tisdall Farrell

entities.name: Alf Bergan
entities.body: One of the two Bloom would take his oath wrote the U. p: up postcard for a lark in the Scotch house. Be a feast for the gods, he thinks, to see Breen take it round to a solicitor.

entities.name: Lizzie Twigg
entities.body: Whose answer to the advertisement said that her literary efforts had had the good fortune to meet with the approval of the eminent poet A. E. No time to do her hair, Bloom decides, drinking sloppy tea with a book of poetry — and then thinks he sees her walking beside the beard and bicycle, taking it all in and not saying a word.

entities.name: James Carlisle
entities.body: Who made the Irish Times: six and a half per cent dividend, a big deal on Coates’s shares. Ca’ canny. Cunning old Scotch hunks.

entities.name: Lady Mountcashel
entities.body: Who has quite recovered after her confinement and rode out with the Ward Union staghounds at the enlargement yesterday at Rathoath, in the paragraph of the Irish Field that sets Bloom off on horsey women. First to the meet and in at the death.

entities.name: Mrs Miriam Dandrade
entities.body: Divorced Spanish American, who sold Bloom her old wraps and black underclothes in the Shelbourne hotel and did not take a feather out of him handling them. As if I was her clotheshorse. Born courtesan; no nursery work for her, thanks.

entities.name: The woman at the Grosvenor
entities.body: The stylish one Bloom watched that morning getting up on the car outside the hotel, silk flash rich stockings white, until the tram slewed between. Up with her on the car: wishswish. She comes back to him here as one of the weightcarrying huntresses, and he cannot place who she was like until he gets Mrs Dandrade.

entities.name: The pugnosed driver
entities.body: Whose tramcar honked its gong and slewed between Bloom and the woman at the Grosvenor that morning. Curse your noisy pugnose. Think that pugnosed driver did it out of spite, he decides now.

entities.name: Stubbs
entities.body: The park ranger who got Bloom in among the viceregal party, where he poured mayonnaise on the plums thinking it was custard.

entities.name: Whelan
entities.body: Of the Express, through whom Stubbs worked Bloom into the viceregal party. Scavenging what the quality left: high tea, and mayonnaise on the plums.

entities.name: Mrs Moisel
entities.body: Big at the same time as Molly: funny sight two of them together, their bellies out. Mothers’ meeting.

entities.name: Old Tom Wall
entities.body: Old Tom Wall, in the one thing Bloom remembers about him: his son crushed Mrs Thornton’s hand being born, with a head like a prize pumpkin.

entities.name: Old Tom Wall’s son
entities.body: His first bow to the public, and the one baby in Mrs Thornton’s long career who did her an injury.

entities.name: Dr Murren
entities.body: Snuffy, knocked up at all hours — for God’ sake, doctor, wife in her throes — and then kept waiting months for his fee. Humane doctors, most of them, Bloom allows.

entities.name: Apjohn
entities.body: One of the boys up in the trees near Goose green playing the monkeys, when they called Bloom Mackerel.

entities.name: Owen Goldberg
entities.body: The third of them in the trees near Goose green, with Apjohn and Bloom, playing the monkeys. A Jewish schoolfellow, and one of the few names from the boyhood Bloom almost never goes back to.

entities.name: Tommy Moore
entities.body: Under whose roguish finger Bloom crosses. They did right to put him up over a urinal: meeting of the waters. The modern edition calls him Tom Moore and spells out the joke.

entities.name: Julia Morkan
entities.body: Whose great song The meeting of the waters was, and who kept her voice up to the very last.

entities.name: Michael Balfe
entities.body: The composer of The Bohemian Girl, whose pupil Julia Morkan was — wasn’t she? Bloom is not sure, and leaves the question hanging as he walks on.

entities.name: Jack Power’s father
entities.body: A G man, which is why Jack Power could a tale unfold about what the police do to a fellow in the bridewell who gives them trouble being lagged.

entities.name: The horsepoliceman
entities.body: Who got a run for his money the day Joe Chamberlain was given his degree in Trinity, his horse’s hoofs clattering after Bloom down Abbey street until he came a wallop on the cobblestones. Must have cracked his skull. Bloom dived into Manning’s and was not souped.

entities.name: Joe Chamberlain
entities.body: Given his degree in Trinity, with the medicals and the Trinity jibs out for trouble and the students yelling that they will hang him on a sourapple tree. Up the Boers.

entities.name: De Wet
entities.body: The Boer general the students cheer in the same breath as they threaten to hang Joe Chamberlain. Three cheers for De Wet: the war is two years over and the slogans are still on the street.

entities.name: Dixon
entities.body: The young medical who dressed the bee sting for Bloom in the Mater, and is now in Holles street where Mrs Purefoy is. Wheels within wheels.

entities.name: Harvey Duff
entities.body: The informer of Boucicault’s play, whose name has become the thing itself: Corny Kelleher he has Harvey Duff in his eye. The modern edition glosses it — a Harvey Duff, an informer — where Joyce lets the name carry it.

entities.name: Mary
entities.body: The slavey at the backdoor in the scene Bloom runs off in his head, ironing with her fat arms while the plainclothes man works round to what the young master was saying. Are those yours, Mary? There are great times coming, Mary. Ah, gelong with your great times coming.

entities.name: The turnkey’s daughter
entities.body: Who got James Stephens out of Richmond, and off from Lusk, while he put up in the Buckingham Palace hotel under their very noses.

entities.name: Garibaldi
entities.body: The one word Bloom adds to James Stephens’s escape, for the kind of fascination it takes to carry a thing like that off — the same fascination he then finds in Parnell.

entities.name: John Howard Parnell
entities.body: The brother, city marshal, who passes Walter Sexton’s window unseeing, like a man walking in his sleep, and will drop into the D.B.C. for his coffee and play chess there. Image of him. Haunting face. They say he never put on the uniform since he got the job, and David Sheehy beat him for south Meath. His brother used men as pawns.

entities.name: Charley Kavanagh
entities.body: The city marshal before him, who used to come out on his high horse: cocked hat, puffed, powdered and shaved. Set against the woebegone walk of the man who has the job now.

entities.name: Mad Fanny
entities.body: One of the sisters, driving about with scarlet harness. All a bit touched: that’s the fascination, the name.

entities.name: Mrs Dickinson
entities.body: The other sister, in the same carriage with the scarlet harness. Bloom sets the two of them beside the brother as evidence that the whole family is a bit touched.

entities.name: Surgeon M’Ardle
entities.body: The surgeon whose bolt upright carriage is the comparison for the two Parnell sisters driving about Dublin. A name Bloom reaches for to fix a posture, and drops again.

entities.name: David Sheehy
entities.body: Who beat John Howard Parnell for south Meath, so that the beaten man applied for the Chiltern Hundreds and retired into public life.

entities.name: The reverend Dr Salmon
entities.body: Provost of Trinity, tinned salmon, well tinned in there. Bloom would not live in the provost’s house if they paid him: like a mortuary chapel.

entities.name: Kerwan
entities.body: Whose mushroom houses are built of breeze, at the end of the passage where the cities pile up and wear away age after age. Shelter, for the night.

entities.name: Young Sinclair
entities.body: At old Harris’s, a wellmannered fellow, with whom Bloom thinks of dropping in for a chat about getting his old fieldglasses set right. Probably at his lunch.

entities.name: Old Harris
entities.body: The optician on Nassau street, old Harris, whose window Bloom would go into for a chat about his old fieldglasses if young Sinclair were not probably at his lunch.

entities.name: Professor Joly
entities.body: At Dunsink, to whom Bloom would like an introduction, or else to learn up something about his family: a man always feels complimented. Lay it on with a trowel. Not go in and blurt out what’s parallax.

entities.name: Pat Kinsella
entities.body: Of the Harp theatre, with his harvestmoon face in a poky bonnet doing the Dion Boucicault business and showing long red pantaloons under his skirts. More power, Pat. Where is he now? Beggar somewhere.

entities.name: Whitbred
entities.body: Who ran the Queen’s theatre after Pat Kinsella’s Harp, in the succession of Dublin stages Bloom counts off while he asks himself how time flies.

entities.name: Dion Boucicault
entities.body: The playwright whose business Kinsella did on the boards of the Harp: harvestmoon face, poky bonnet, long red pantaloons under the skirts. Harvey Duff, four paragraphs earlier, is out of the same author.

entities.name: Meyerbeer
entities.body: Whose chorus comes up out of the flood of bloodhued poplin in Brown Thomas’s window. La causa è santa. Tara tara. Great chorus that.

entities.name: Cormac
entities.body: The last pagan king of Ireland in the schoolpoem, who choked himself at Sletty southward of the Boyne. Wonder what he was eating. Saint Patrick converted him to Christianity; couldn’t swallow it all however.

entities.name: The illgirt server
entities.body: Gathering the sticky clattering plates in the Burton while Bloom stands in the doorway with his gorge rising.

entities.name: Rock
entities.body: The head bailiff, standing at the bar of the Burton blowing the foamy crown from his tankard. Well up: it splashed yellow near his boot.

entities.name: Father O’Flynn
entities.body: Of the song, who would make hares of them all — Bloom’s guess at who would keep order in the communal kitchen of the future.

entities.name: The old woman that lived in a shoe
entities.body: She had so many children: the rhyme Bloom reaches for over Mrs Purefoy’s three days, next to queen Victoria’s nine and the twilight sleep she was given.

entities.name: Ham
entities.body: Noah’s son, in the pun Bloom makes over Davy Byrne’s shelves: ham and his descendants musterred and bred there.

entities.name: Mr MacTrigger
entities.body: Of the comic song about the right royal old nigger who ate the somethings of him, which keeps surfacing while Bloom eats his cheese sandwich. His five hundred wives. Had the time of their lives. It grew bigger and bigger and bigger. Both of his appearances stand in Gutenberg italics in the older edition, which is why the name is keyed and not aliased.

entities.name: Nosey Flynn
entities.body: In his nook in Davy Byrne’s, snuffling, scratching his groin, with a dewdrop on the end of his nose that Bloom watches all through the sandwich. He is the one who says Blazes Boylan is mixed up in the tour, and the one who tells Davy Byrne, when Bloom goes out to the yard, that he is in the craft: ancient free and accepted order, they give him a leg up.

entities.name: Davy Byrne
entities.body: Moral pub, Bloom calls it: he doesn’t chat, stands a drink now and then but in leapyear once in four, and cashed a cheque for him once. He comes forward from the hindbar in tuckstitched shirtsleeves, will never put anything on a horse, and says of Bloom, decent quiet man he is, I never once saw him over the line.

entities.name: The curate
entities.body: Who serves the burgundy and the gorgonzola sandwich. Seven d., sir. Thank you, sir. The modern edition calls him the barman.

entities.name: Jack Mooney
entities.body: Who told Nosey Flynn about the slice of luck Boylan had over the boxingmatch, and so put the whole story into Davy Byrne’s with Bloom standing there eating his sandwich.

entities.name: Myler Keogh
entities.body: Who won that match against the soldier in the Portobello barracks. Boylan had him down in the county Carlow for near a month before it came off, sucking duck eggs by God till further orders, and kept him off the boose.

entities.name: The soldier in the Portobello barracks
entities.body: The man Myler Keogh beat in the barracks, on whom Boylan had his slice of luck. The episode gives him no name and nobody in the pub asks for one.

entities.name: Lord Howard de Walden
entities.body: Whose Zinfandel is the favourite for the Gold cup, having won at Epsom. The race is run this afternoon and is on every tongue in the pub.

entities.name: Morny Cannon
entities.body: The jockey riding Zinfandel for the Gold cup, in the tip Nosey Flynn passes on as though it were his own.

entities.name: Rothschild
entities.body: Whose filly it was that won in a thunderstorm with wadding in her ears, blue jacket and yellow cap, in the race Nosey Flynn could have got seven to one on.

entities.name: The archduke Leopold
entities.body: One of those Habsburgs, in the story Bloom half remembers about eating the scruff off his own head — or was it Otto. It comes up between the fifty-year-old Chinese eggs and the idea for a poison mystery.

entities.name: Otto
entities.body: The other name Bloom tries for the same Habsburg story, and does not settle either. One of those Habsburgs, he decides, and goes on to the man who ate the scruff off his own head.

entities.name: Micky Hanlon
entities.body: Of Moore street, who ripped the guts out of fish and made money hand over fist and cannot write his name on a cheque: you would think he was painting the landscape with his mouth twisted. Ignorant as a kish of brogues, worth fifty thousand pounds.

entities.name: Miss Dubedat
entities.body: Of the waiter’s patter Bloom runs in his head — may I tempt you to a little more filleted lemon sole, miss Dubedat? Yes, do bedad. And she did bedad — and then of the real one who lived in Killiney. Huguenot name, he expects.

entities.name: Coffey the butcher
entities.body: Who has the right to venisons of the forest, in the list of things that go by rank: royal sturgeon to the high sheriff, and half a cow sent back to his excellency.

entities.name: Venus
entities.body: One of the naked goddesses standing in the round hall of the museum. Curves are beauty; curves the world admires. They don’t care what man looks.

entities.name: Juno
entities.body: The second of the naked goddesses in the round hall. Lovely forms of women sculped Junonian. Immortal lovely, and never speaking: they don’t care what man looks.

entities.name: Pygmalion
entities.body: Whose statue came alive, in the question Bloom puts to himself in front of them: suppose she did Pygmalion and Galatea, what would she say first? Mortal! Put you in your proper place.

entities.name: Galatea
entities.body: The statue Pygmalion made and loved, who came alive. Bloom gives her the first word and makes it a rebuke: Mortal! Put you in your proper place.

entities.name: Tom Rochford
entities.body: Who comes into Davy Byrne’s frowning with a hand on his claret waistcoat, asks for a glass of fresh water, and tips a twisted paper of powder into it for that cursed dyspepsia. Wonder if he will do anything with that invention of his, Bloom thinks afterwards: wasting time explaining it to Flynn’s mouth.

entities.name: John Wyse Nolan
entities.body: Whose wife has the Irish farm dairy in Henry street, where Nosey Flynn met Bloom coming out with a jar of cream for his better half.

entities.name: John Wyse Nolan’s wife
entities.body: Who keeps the dairy. The cream is the whole of Flynn’s argument that Bloom does not live on the ads he picks up.

entities.name: The saint Leger of Doneraile
entities.body: The one woman, Nosey Flynn says, who hid herself in a clock to find out what the masons do be doing — and they smelt her out and swore her in on the spot a master mason.

entities.name: Peeping Tom
entities.body: Through the keyhole: the figure Bloom reaches for in the business of plainclothes men courting slaveys. Decoy duck.

entities.name: The loafer against John Long’s
entities.body: Lounging in heavy thought, gnawing a crusted knuckle. Handy man wants job. Small wages. Will eat anything.

entities.name: The reverend Thomas Connellan
entities.body: Whose bookstore Bloom passes, with Why I left the church of Rome in the window, and the Birds’ Nest beside it. Women run him. Same bait as the soup given to pauper children in the time of the blight, and as the society across the way that papa went to for the conversion of poor jews.

entities.name: The blind stripling
entities.body: Tapping the curbstone with his slender cane at the Dawson street crossing, who wants to go to Molesworth street and South Frederick street. Bloom tells him about the van that is not moving, touches the thin elbow and takes the limp seeing hand across, tries a common remark about the rain, and gets Thanks, sir. Knows I’m a man. Voice.

entities.name: Penrose
entities.body: The priestylooking chap with the weak eyes who was always squinting in when Bloom passed, and stopped at Citron’s on saint Kevin’s parade. Bloom cannot get the name in the morning — Pen something. Pendennis? — and it comes back to him behind the blind man in the afternoon.

entities.name: William Miller
entities.body: Plumber, whose window of bare clean closestools turns Bloom’s thoughts back inside himself: swallow a pin, tour round the body, and the poor buffer standing all the time with his insides on show. Science.

entities.name: Don Giovanni
entities.body: Whom the statue invites to supper, in the line Bloom hums going up Dawson street: Don Giovanni, a cenar teco m’invitasti. He tries it in English and it doesn’t go properly, and stops on the one word he wants: what does that teco mean? Tonight perhaps.

entities.name: Billy Prescott
entities.body: Of the dyeworks, whose ad would bring Bloom to two fifteen if he gets it. Five guineas about. On the pig’s back.

entities.name: Sir Frederick Falkiner
entities.body: Recorder of Dublin, going into the freemasons’ hall solemn as Troy after his good lunch in Earlsfort terrace, with the tales of the bench and the assizes and I sentenced him to ten years. Wellmeaning old man, and the devil on moneylenders: he gave Reuben J a great strawcalling.

entities.name: His Excellency the lord lieutenant
entities.body: On the placard for the Mirus bazaar, sixteenth of June, in aid of funds for Mercer’s hospital. Bloom thinks of going out to Ballsbridge on the strength of it and dropping in on Keyes: sure to know someone on the gate.

entities.name: Handel
entities.body: Whose Messiah was first given in aid of Mercer’s hospital, which the Mirus bazaar is being held for now. Yes. Handel.

entities.name: Sir Thomas Deane
entities.body: Who designed the museum, and whose cream curves of stone Bloom stares at, heart quopping, while he turns out his pockets at the gate. Handsome building. Sir Thomas Deane was the Greek architecture.

entities.name: The farmer’s daughter
entities.body: Whose bag Bloom had to pick up and hand to her at Limerick junction, travelling to Ennis last year, in the list of what people leave behind them in trains and cloakrooms.

entities.name: The Egyptian highpriest
entities.body: Whose speech to the youthful Moses John F Taylor reported in episode 7 — the voice raised in a tone of like haughtiness and like pride, setting Isis and Osiris, Horus and Ammon Ra against the local and obscure idol of the Jews. Stephen hears it again in the silence of the library: and I heard the voice of that Egyptian highpriest.

entities.name: Aubrey
entities.body: John Aubrey, whose Brief Lives is the authority for Shakespeare having held horses at the playhouse door: how else could Aubrey’s ostler and callboy get rich quick? Not the Aubrey of Magdalen whom Mulligan quotes in episode 1.

entities.name: Mr Lyster
entities.body: The quaker librarian, urbane and creaking, who purrs about Wilhelm Meister, tiptoes in and out on his neatsleather all through the argument, and is called away three times — by an attendant, by a gentleman from the Freeman, and by Father Dineen. Most zealous, most fair, most kind, most honest broadbrim. He is the one who asks Stephen outright whether he thinks she was unfaithful to the poet.

entities.name: John Eglinton
entities.body: W. K. Magee, who signs himself John Eglinton, editing Dana: the carping voice of the room, with active eyebrows, a spare body and a sizar’s stern frown. He makes his blood boil to hear Aristotle compared with Plato, will not have his belief shaken that Shakespeare is Hamlet, and tells Stephen at the end that he is a delusion who has brought them all this way to show them a French triangle. Stephen names him eight ways in one afternoon — littlejohn, Judge, Second, Steadfast John, Eclecticon, Eglintonus Chronolologos, Eglinton Johannes, Magee.

entities.name: Mr Best
entities.body: Tall, young, mild, light, with a new large clean bright notebook, who says don’t you know at every turn and cares more for the light touch than for the argument. He brings in Mallarmé and the prose poems, the brother motive in Grimm, and the story of Mr W. H., and he hopes Stephen will say a good word for Richard, don’t you know, for his sake.

entities.name: The attendant
entities.body: Noiseless at the door, who sets it open but slightly and beckons Mr Lyster out with a noiseless beck; who brings in the card from the Freeman; and who calls from the doorway that Father Dineen wants him.

entities.name: Evans
entities.body: The attendant Mr Lyster calls to conduct the gentleman from the Freeman to the provincial papers.

entities.name: Father Dineen
entities.body: Who wants Mr Lyster, and takes him out of the room at the one moment when the quaker librarian has asked the question he most wants answered.

entities.name: Goethe
entities.body: Of the priceless pages of Wilhelm Meister, the great poet on a great brother poet, whose judgments Mr Lyster always feels are so true. True in the larger analysis. Stephen gives him back later in a harder saying that Mr Magee likes to quote: beware of what you wish for in youth, because you will get it in middle life.

entities.name: Monsieur de la Palice
entities.body: Who was alive fifteen minutes before his death — Stephen’s sneer at the quaker librarian’s larger analysis, out of the French song about the obvious.

entities.name: Yeats
entities.body: The shining seven, W.B. calls them. He admired Colum’s line about the Grecian vase in the wild earth, and Mulligan asks Stephen at the end why he could not have done the Yeats touch on Lady Gregory’s book instead of slating it.

entities.name: Messer Brunetto
entities.body: Brunetto Latini, Dante’s master, from whom Stephen takes the word for John Eglinton’s stare: a basilisk — and when the serpent sees the man, it poisons him. Messer Brunetto, I thank thee for the word.

entities.name: Kathleen
entities.body: Gaptoothed Kathleen, her four beautiful green fields and the stranger in her house: Ireland herself in the play, whom Cranly’s eleven true Wicklowmen were to free. The modern edition writes Kathleen Ireland and takes the riddle out of it.

entities.name: Ben Jonson
entities.body: Old Ben, who admired Shakespeare on this side idolatry. The older edition gives only the first name, as John Eglinton would say it among people who know; the modern edition supplies the surname.

entities.name: James I
entities.body: One of the three men the schools have proposed as the real author of Hamlet, in Russell’s list of the questions he thinks purely academic. He returns unnamed at 9:294 as the Scotch philosophaster with a turn for witchroasting whose accession is dated by Hamlet and Macbeth.

entities.name: Essex
entities.body: The second of them.

entities.name: Gustave Moreau
entities.body: Whose painting is the painting of ideas, in Russell’s argument that art has to reveal formless spiritual essences and not the poet’s drinking and the poet’s debts.

entities.name: Shelley
entities.body: Whose deepest poetry brings the mind into contact with the eternal wisdom, Russell says; and whose figure of the mind as a fading coal Stephen turns against him, in the intense instant of imagination. Mulligan quotes him too over the foamborn Aphrodite: life of life, thy lips enkindle.

entities.name: Plato
entities.body: The other half of the argument. Aristotle was once Plato’s schoolboy, Stephen says, and has remained so, John Eglinton hopes; and which of the two would have banished me from his commonwealth? Hamlet’s monologue on the afterlife of his princely soul is as shallow as Plato’s, and the dialogues are the form Mr Best thinks the theory ought to take, like the Platonic dialogues Wilde wrote.

entities.name: Dunlop
entities.body: First of the theosophists in Stephen’s silent catalogue of the Dublin lodge: Daniel Nicol Dunlop, of the yogibogeybox in Dawson chambers.

entities.name: Judge
entities.body: The noblest Roman of them all, second in the same list.

entities.name: K. H.
entities.body: Their master, whose identity is no secret to adepts: the mahatma the Dublin theosophists took their instruction from.

entities.name: Mrs Cooper Oakley
entities.body: Who once glimpsed our very illustrious sister H. P. B.’s elemental — the story that makes Stephen break out in mock scandal: you naughtn’t to look, missus, when a lady’s ashowing of her elemental.

entities.name: Sophia
entities.body: Repentant sophia, departed to the plane of buddhi: the fallen wisdom of the gnostic scheme, bridesister to the Christ in the theosophical account Stephen is mocking.

entities.name: Jubainville
entities.body: Whose book Mr Best was showing Haines when Haines got enthusiastic about the Lovesongs of Connacht and went off to Gill’s to buy them: d’Arbois de Jubainville on the Irish mythological cycle.

entities.name: Hyde
entities.body: Douglas Hyde, whose Lovesongs of Connacht Haines has gone to buy, and whose own verse — bound thee forth, my booklet, quick, to greet the callous public — Stephen recites in his head, lean unlovely English and all.

entities.name: Mallarmé
entities.body: The finest flower of corruption France produces, in Russell’s judgment; and to Mr Best the author of the wonderful prose poems Stephen MacKenna used to read to him in Paris, including the one about Hamlet: il se promène, lisant au livre de lui-même.

entities.name: Homer
entities.body: Whose Phæacians live the desirable life revealed only to the poor of heart, Russell says; and whom Mulligan invokes at the end, chanting Longworth’s puff of Lady Gregory: the most beautiful book that has come out of our country in my time. One thinks of Homer.

entities.name: Stephen MacKenna
entities.body: Who used to read Mallarmé’s prose poems to Mr Best in Paris.

entities.name: Robert Greene
entities.body: Who called Shakespeare a deathsman of the soul — the phrase Stephen opens the argument with. The modern edition turns it round and calls him a death-dealer of the soul.

entities.name: The fat boy in Pickwick
entities.body: Who wants to make your flesh creep, and is John Eglinton’s comparison for Stephen insisting that Hamlet is a ghoststory.

entities.name: King Hamlet
entities.body: The ghost from limbo patrum, returning to the world that has forgotten him. Who is King Hamlet? is the question the whole theory turns on, and Stephen’s answer is Shakespeare himself, playing the part in his own play and speaking his own son’s name to the young player in front of him.

entities.name: Drake
entities.body: Whose canvasclimbers chew their sausages among the groundlings at the Globe, in the hour of a day in mid June that Stephen builds for them.

entities.name: Burbage
entities.body: The young player who stands before the ghost beyond the rack of cerecloth and is called Hamlet. He returns in the story out of Manningham: the burgher’s wife who bade Dick Burbage to her bed after she had seen him in Richard III, and Shakespeare answering from the capon’s blankets that William the conqueror came before Richard III.

entities.name: Hamnet Shakespeare
entities.body: The son of his body, dead in Stratford at eleven, whose namesake lives for ever. Had Hamnet lived he would have been prince Hamlet’s twin; and Hamlet, the black prince, is Hamnet Shakespeare.

entities.name: Ann Hathaway
entities.body: Ann Shakespeare, born Hathaway, whom Stephen will not let the room forget. Eight years older than the boy she tumbled in the cornfield, sweet and twentysix; she bore his children, laid pennies on his eyes, and got the secondbest bed. She died, Stephen says, sixtyseven years after she was born — and of the thirtyfour years between the day she married him and the day she buried him, the plays say nothing except what he branded her with in the fifth scene of Hamlet.

entities.name: Villiers de l’Isle
entities.body: Who said that as for living our servants can do that for us — Russell’s authority for refusing to pry into the family life of a great man.

entities.name: Georgina Johnson
entities.body: The clergyman’s daughter in whose bed Stephen spent most of the pound Russell lent him when he was hungry. Agenbite of inwit.

entities.name: Socrates
entities.body: Who learnt dialectic from Xanthippe and from his mother how to bring thoughts into the world, and whom neither the midwife’s lore nor the caudlelectures saved from the archons and their naggin of hemlock. Stephen uses him twice more: Shakespeare had a midwife to mother as he had a shrew to wife; and Maeterlinck’s if Socrates leave his house today he will find the sage seated on his doorstep.

entities.name: Xanthippe
entities.body: His wife, and John Eglinton’s example of a shrew who was not a useful portal of discovery.

entities.name: Myrto
entities.body: His other wife, absit nomen — what he learnt from her, Stephen says, no man, not a woman, will ever know.

entities.name: Katharine the shrew
entities.body: Whom Hortensio calls young and beautiful, against the room’s assumption that the woman Shakespeare married must have been the ugliest doxy in all Warwickshire.

entities.name: Hortensio
entities.body: Who calls her so.

entities.name: Adonis
entities.body: The boy the greyeyed goddess bends over, stooping to conquer — and in Stephen’s reading a boldfaced Stratford wench tumbling a lover younger than herself in a cornfield. The poem’s title at the head of the same sentence is a book and carries no card.

entities.name: Piper
entities.body: Back from Berlin and coming to Moore’s tonight, which is the news that makes Mr Best pipe. He is the man who met Herr Bleibtreu and brought home the Rutland theory.

entities.name: Louis H. Victory
entities.body: One of the two poets Stephen lists among the faithful hermetists waiting for the light, ripe for chelaship.

entities.name: T. Caulfield Irwin
entities.body: The other.

entities.name: Colum
entities.body: Young Colum, whose Drover Russell liked and in whose line about the Grecian vase Yeats found that queer thing genius. One of the younger poets whose verses Russell is gathering into a sheaf.

entities.name: Starkey
entities.body: Another of them, whom Russell twice tells Stephen to bring along tonight.

entities.name: George Roberts
entities.body: Who is doing the commercial part of the anthology.

entities.name: Longworth
entities.body: Editor of the Express, who will give the sheaf a good puff — and who is awfully sick, Mulligan says, after what Stephen wrote about Lady Gregory’s book in his paper.

entities.name: Moore
entities.body: George Moore, at whose house they are all going tonight, and whom Miss Mitchell’s joke makes Martyn’s wild oats. Our national epic has yet to be written and Moore is the man for it: a knight of the rueful countenance here in Dublin. Mulligan closes the episode on him — Monsieur Moore, lecturer on French letters to the youth of Ireland. Not the Tommy Moore of episode 8 nor Moore street.

entities.name: Martyn
entities.body: Edward Martyn, the other half of the joke, and Sancho to Moore’s Quixote.

entities.name: Miss Mitchell
entities.body: Whose joke it was. Awfully clever, isn’t it?

entities.name: Don Quixote
entities.body: Whom Moore and Martyn remind one of.

entities.name: Sancho Panza
entities.body: And his squire.

entities.name: Dulcinea
entities.body: And his lady — and who would she be, in the Dublin version of the joke?

entities.name: Dr Sigerson
entities.body: Who says our national epic has yet to be written.

entities.name: O’Neill Russell
entities.body: Proposed for the saffron kilt and the grand old tongue. Not the Russell of this episode, who is A. E.

entities.name: James Stephens
entities.body: Who is doing some clever sketches. We are becoming important, it seems. Not the head centre of the Fenians whom Bloom and Kevin Egan remember.

entities.name: Cordelia
entities.body: Cordoglio. Lir’s loneliest daughter — the one word Stephen answers Russell’s literary evening with, having just handed over Mr Deasy’s letter and been given nothing.

entities.name: Lir
entities.body: Whose loneliest daughter she is. The older edition writes Lir, the Irish sea god whose children were turned into swans; the modern edition writes Lear and makes it Shakespeare’s king. Joyce’s line holds both at once.

entities.name: Mr Norman
entities.body: Editor of the Irish Homestead, to whom Russell will give Mr Deasy’s letter if he considers it important. We have so much correspondence. Not the Connolly Norman of episode 1.

entities.name: Synge
entities.body: Who has promised Russell an article for Dana; who writes as Shakespeare does, Mulligan says; who is out in pampooties to murder Stephen for pissing on his halldoor in Glasthule; and who has left off wearing black to be like nature.

entities.name: Mother Dana
entities.body: The goddess who weaves and unweaves, in Stephen’s figure for the artist weaving and unweaving his image out of new stuff time after time. The modern edition writes Mother Nature and loses her; the magazine of the same name, which Russell and Fred Ryan write for, is not she.

entities.name: Drummond of Hawthornden
entities.body: Who helped Stephen over that stile, he admits to himself the moment the figure is out of his mouth.

entities.name: Renan
entities.body: Who admired the plays of Shakespeare’s later years so much, and the play — the Tempest — written after the Sea Venture came home from Bermudas with Patsy Caliban aboard.

entities.name: Ulysses
entities.body: Tried, like another Ulysses: the shipwrecked man whose heart is softened when a child, a girl, is placed in his arms. He turns up again as the man Moore makes quote Aristotle on the seacoast of Bohemia.

entities.name: Pericles
entities.body: Prince of Tyre, in whose arms Marina is placed.

entities.name: Marina
entities.body: A child of storm, the daughter given back to him. My dearest wife, Pericles says, was like this maid.

entities.name: Miranda
entities.body: A wonder: the second of the three daughters of the late plays, between Marina and Perdita, in Stephen’s list of what was lost and given back.

entities.name: Perdita
entities.body: That which was lost.

entities.name: Bacon
entities.body: Good Bacon: gone musty. Shakespeare Bacon’s wild oats, and the cypherjugglers going the highroads after him — the first of the four names Stephen runs together into Rutlandbaconsouthamptonshakespeare.

entities.name: Mr Brandes
entities.body: Georg Brandes, who accepts Pericles as the first play of the closing period.

entities.name: Mr Sidney Lee
entities.body: Or Mr Simon Lazarus, as some aver his name is — John Eglinton’s way of asking what the other authority says.

entities.name: Mr George Bernard Shaw
entities.body: Another Irish commentator the quaker librarian thinks they ought to mention.

entities.name: Mr Frank Harris
entities.body: Whose articles on Shakespeare in the Saturday Review were surely brilliant, and who too draws an unhappy relation with the dark lady of the sonnets. Not the old Harris of Nassau street whose fieldglasses Bloom means to have seen to.

entities.name: The dark lady of the sonnets
entities.body: Whom the commentators keep finding, and whose favoured rival, on Frank Harris’s reading, is William Herbert.

entities.name: William Herbert
entities.body: Earl of Pembroke: the favoured rival. If the poet must be rejected, the quaker librarian owns, such a rejection would seem more in harmony with our notions of what ought not to have been.

entities.name: Lucrece
entities.body: Whose bluecircled ivory globes are the first of the two the ghost’s speech is always turned back towards.

entities.name: Imogen
entities.body: And the second: her breast, bare, with its mole cinquespotted.

entities.name: Johann Most
entities.body: Third in the brood of mockers — Photius, pseudomalachi, Johann Most — whose blasphemy Stephen answers with the whole creed run together in one breath.

entities.name: Vining
entities.body: Who held that the prince was a woman.

entities.name: Judge Barton
entities.body: Who is searching for some clues that Hamlet was an Irishman: he swears — His Highness, not His Lordship — by saint Patrick.

entities.name: Willie Hughes
entities.body: A man all hues, for whom Wilde proves the sonnets were written in the Portrait of Mr W. H. Or Hughie Wills, Stephen thinks: Mr William Himself. W. H.: who am I?

entities.name: Jove
entities.body: A cool ruttime send them: the one line of Blake’s pairing time that Stephen turns on the blond ephebe in front of him. Everywhere else in this book the name is only the exclamation.

entities.name: Aphrodite
entities.body: The foamborn, whom Mulligan went over to the museum to hail, and to whom he says we must do homage every day. The Greek mouth that has never been twisted in prayer.

entities.name: Griselda
entities.body: Patient Griselda, one of the two figures the room had settled Mrs Shakespeare into before Stephen began — the other being a Penelope stayathome.

entities.name: Walt Whitman
entities.body: Who called it the art of feudalism; Stephen calls Shakespeare’s the art of surfeit.

entities.name: Sir Walter Raleigh
entities.body: Who, when they arrested him, had half a million francs on his back including a pair of fancy stays.

entities.name: Eliza Tudor
entities.body: The gombeenwoman, who had underlinen enough to vie with her of Sheba; and again, at the end of the same speech, fay Elizabeth, otherwise carrotty Bess, the gross virgin who inspired the Merry Wives. The modern edition writes Queen Elizabeth both times.

entities.name: Her of Sheba
entities.body: The queen whose wardrobe is the comparison. The modern edition names her the Queen of Sheba.

entities.name: Manningham
entities.body: Whose story of the burgher’s wife, Dick Burbage and William the conqueror Stephen retells to prove the twenty years were not chaste.

entities.name: Mistress Fitton
entities.body: The gay lakin, mount and cry O — one of the women the sonnets have been fitted to.

entities.name: Sir William Davenant
entities.body: Of Oxford — or rather his mother, with her cup of canary for any cockcanary.

entities.name: Blessed Margaret Mary
entities.body: Margaret Mary Alacoque, of the Sacred Heart, whose name Mulligan turns into a piece of filth with his pious eyes upturned. The modern edition writes Margaret Mary Whatshername and keeps the shape of the joke without the word.

entities.name: Harry of six wives
entities.body: Whose daughter is one of the lady friends in Stephen’s list. The modern edition writes King Henry.

entities.name: Gerard
entities.body: The herbalist of Fetter lane, in whose rosery Shakespeare walks greyedauburn in the one wholly quiet paragraph of this episode.

entities.name: Shylock
entities.body: Whom Shakespeare drew out of his own long pocket: the son of a maltjobber and moneylender who was himself a cornjobber and moneylender, and exacted his pound of flesh in interest for every money lent.

entities.name: Chettle
entities.body: Falstaff, who reported his uprightness of dealing — the divers of worship among his borrowers.

entities.name: Falstaff
entities.body: The fat knight, whom John Eglinton feels is his supreme creation, and who was not a family man.

entities.name: Lopez
entities.body: The queen’s leech, hanged and quartered, his jew’s heart plucked forth while he was yet alive: the jewbaiting that Shylock chimes with.

entities.name: Sidney
entities.body: Whose sugared sonnets Shakespeare’s follow, and out of whose Arcadia the underplot of King Lear in which Edmund figures is lifted and spatchcocked on to a Celtic legend older than history. Not the Mr Sidney Lee of 9:174.

entities.name: Coleridge
entities.body: Who called him myriadminded — Mr Best’s one contribution to the case for the defence.

entities.name: Pallas Athena
entities.body: Who came out of her father’s head, and whom Mulligan invokes when he announces that he is big with child: I have an unborn child in my brain. A play! Let me parturiate!

entities.name: Volumnia
entities.body: Whose scene in Coriolanus came out of the death of Shakespeare’s mother.

entities.name: Young Arthur
entities.body: Whose deathscene in King John came out of his boyson’s death.

entities.name: Cleopatra
entities.body: Fleshpot of Egypt: one of the three Stephen says we may guess at, where the girls of the late plays we know. The play named a hundred lines earlier is a book and carries no card.

entities.name: Cressid
entities.body: The second of the three. The modern edition spells her Cressida.

entities.name: Gilbert Shakespeare
entities.body: The brother who is nowhere in the works: in his old age he told some cavaliers that he once got a pass for nowt from Maister Gatherer and saw his brud Maister Wull up in Lunnon in a wrastling play. The playhouse sausage filled Gilbert’s soul.

entities.name: Edmund Shakespeare
entities.body: The brother who lay dying in Southwark while King Lear was being written, and whose name went to the bastard in it.

entities.name: Richard Shakespeare
entities.body: The third brother, whose name went to the crookback. Stephen keeps him and Edmund for the last and calls them, with his own uncle Richie Goulding folded into the joke, those two noble kinsmen nuncle Richie and nuncle Edmund.

entities.name: Richard Crookback
entities.body: A whoreson crookback, misbegotten, who makes love to a widowed Ann and wins her; the only king of all his kings unshielded by Shakespeare’s reverence. Richard the conqueror, third brother, came after William the conquered.

entities.name: Edmund in King Lear
entities.body: The bastard of the underplot, one of the trinity of black Wills with Iago and Richard Crookback: two of the three bear the wicked uncles’ names.

entities.name: John o’Gaunt
entities.body: Whose name was dear to him, as Shakespeare’s own name was dear to Shakespeare. Not the horse Nosey Flynn lost money on in episode 8.

entities.name: Icarus
entities.body: Pater, ait: the boy who flew and fell, and the figure Stephen turns on his own Paris year. Seabedabbled, fallen, weltering.

entities.name: Grimm
entities.body: In whose fairytales Mr Best finds the brother motive too — the third brother that always marries the sleeping beauty and wins the best prize.

entities.name: Stephen’s brother
entities.body: Where is your brother? Apothecaries’ hall. My whetstone — one line, and the only mention of him in the argument about brothers.

entities.name: Esau
entities.body: Whose voice Stephen is tired of hearing come out of his own mouth. My kingdom for a drink.

entities.name: George Meredith
entities.body: Whose novel John Eglinton will not have combined with a Norse saga, and whose Que voulez-vous? Moore would say.

entities.name: Prospero
entities.body: Who breaks his staff, buries it certain fathoms in the earth and drowns his book; and who returns in the epilogue as prosperous Prospero, the good man rewarded.

entities.name: Susan
entities.body: The married daughter, chip of the old block, accused of adultery near the end of his life; and in the list of widows, Susan, her husband too.

entities.name: Judith
entities.body: Her sister: her husband and all her sons.

entities.name: Joan
entities.body: His sister: her four brothers.

entities.name: Mary Shakespeare
entities.body: His mother, whose name lives in the forest of Arden, and whose death brought from him the scene with Volumnia. Mary, her goodman John, at the head of the list of women who saw their men down and under.

entities.name: John Shakespeare
entities.body: His father, in the months after whose death he wrote the play. The corpse of John Shakespeare does not walk the night. From hour to hour it rots and rots.

entities.name: Elizabeth
entities.body: Susan’s daughter, who, to use granddaddy’s words, wed her second having killed her first; and Lizzie, grandpa’s lump of love, in the epilogue.

entities.name: José
entities.body: Who kills the real Carmen — the lover of an ideal or a perversion, in Stephen’s figure for the man who acts and is acted on.

entities.name: Carmen
entities.body: Whom he kills.

entities.name: Dumas fils
entities.body: Or is it Dumas père? — John Eglinton cannot remember which of them said that after God Shakespeare has created most.

entities.name: Dumas père
entities.body: The other one.

entities.name: Maeterlinck
entities.body: Who says that if Socrates leave his house today he will find the sage seated on his doorstep, and if Judas go forth tonight it is to Judas his steps will tend. Mulligan names him again on the stairs, with the Abbey players creating a new art for Europe like the Greeks or M. Maeterlinck.

entities.name: Judas
entities.body: Whose steps tend to himself.

entities.name: Herr Bleibtreu
entities.body: The man Piper met in Berlin, who is working up the Rutland theory and believes the secret is hidden in the Stratford monument. He believes his theory, John Eglinton says, which is more than Stephen will say for his own.

entities.name: The present duke
entities.body: Whom Herr Bleibtreu is going to visit and prove to that his ancestor wrote the plays. It will come as a surprise to his grace.

entities.name: Fresh Nelly
entities.body: One of the two gonorrheal ladies Mulligan says he found the bard Kinch studying the Summa contra Gentiles in the company of; and a character in the play he conceives on the stairs.

entities.name: Rosalie
entities.body: The coalquay whore. The other one.

entities.name: Medical Dick
entities.body: Of the rhyme Mulligan pianos out in the middle of the brothers scene — then outspoke medical Dick to his comrade medical Davy — and of the playbill on the stairs: two birds with one stone.

entities.name: Medical Davy
entities.body: His comrade.

entities.name: Toby Tostoff
entities.body: A ruined Pole. First on the playbill of Everyman His Own Wife, a national immorality in three orgasms, by Ballocky Mulligan.

entities.name: Crab
entities.body: A bushranger. Second on it.

entities.name: Ængus
entities.body: Wandering Ængus of the birds, whom Mulligan calls Stephen on the way out, and whom Stephen has already claimed on the portico: here I watched the birds for augury.

entities.name: F. M’Curdy Atkinson
entities.body: The same that had the wooden leg, in Mulligan’s limerick on the stairs, and one of the two who were there when Longworth got angry.

entities.name: Gregory
entities.body: That old hake Gregory, whose drivel Stephen slated in the Express after she got him the job on the paper. The modern edition gives her the title and writes Lady Gregory.

entities.name: The ancient mariner
entities.body: I fear thee, ancient mariner — Mulligan’s word for Bloom at the door, in the same breath as the wandering jew.

entities.name: The wandering jew
entities.body: Did you see his eye? He looked upon you to lust after you. The figure Mulligan fastens on Bloom as he passes out between them, bowing, greeting.

entities.name: Cymbeline
entities.body: Whose druid priests give Stephen the last words of the episode: laud we the gods, and let our crooked smokes climb to their nostrils from our bless’d altars.

entities.name: Phedo
entities.body: Whose toyable fair hair is Stephen’s word for Mr Best, the douce youngling, minion of pleasure, standing beside the dour recluse.

entities.name: Lousy Lucy
entities.body: Sir Thomas Lucy, who had him whipped for poaching — one of the two things Stephen says Shakespeare forgot no more than he forgot anything. The name is keyed, not aliased: 12:513 is S. Lucy among the saints.

entities.name: Dowden
entities.body: Edward Dowden of Highfield house, the professor whose answer to the charge against the bard was that all we can say is that life ran very high in those days. William Shakespeare and company, limited: the people’s William. For terms apply.

entities.name: Mr Justice Madden
entities.body: In whose Diary of Master William Silence the hunting terms have been found, and whom Mr Lyster is quoting when the attendant interrupts him with Bloom’s card.

entities.name: Oisin
entities.body: Oisin with Patrick: the pagan poet arguing with the saint, which is what Stephen makes of his own quarrelling with Mulligan in Paris, in words of words for words.

entities.name: Thoth
entities.body: God of libraries, a birdgod, moonycrowned, presiding over the coffined thoughts in their mummycases while the room is empty.

entities.name: Achilles
entities.body: What name Achilles bore when he lived among women — one of the things not known that the vestal’s lamp watches over.

entities.name: The soothsayer
entities.body: Whom Cæsar did not believe: what he would have lived to do had he believed him is the first of the possibilities of the possible as possible.

entities.name: Dr Bob Kenny
entities.body: Who is attending Stephen’s mother, in the sentence he hears his father speak on the quayside as he hurries home from Paris to her deathbed.

entities.name: Magee Mor Matthew
entities.body: John Eglinton’s father, as Stephen imagines him coming up from Ultonian Antrim on quarter days: a rugged rough rugheaded kern, in strossers with a buttoned codpiece, his nether stocks bemired with clauber of ten forests. Mr Magee, sir, there’s a gentleman to see you. Me? Says he’s your father, sir.

entities.name: Wordsworth
entities.body: Give me my Wordsworth — what the son says when the father comes up the stairs.

entities.name: Nell Gwynn
entities.body: Don’t forget Nell Gwynn Herpyllis: Stephen’s gloss on the old mistress Aristotle’s will provides for.

entities.name: Herpyllis
entities.body: The mistress herself, whom the dying philosopher bids his friends be kind to and let live in his villa.

entities.name: Boccaccio
entities.body: Whose Calandrino is the one man who ever felt himself with child.

entities.name: Calandrino
entities.body: The first and last such man.

entities.name: The moor
entities.body: The moor in him whom the hornmad Iago ceaselessly wills to suffer: Shakespeare as bawd and cuckold, acting and acted on.
